claim: LCLs are prepared by in vitro transformation of resting primary B cells from peripheral blood with Epstein–Barr virus (EBV).
source: Lymphoblastoid cell lines (LCLs) are immortalized cells prepared by in vitro transformation of resting primary B cells from peripheral blood with Epstein–Barr virus (EBV) (Bird et al., 1981; Anderson and Gusella, 1984).
evidence: This is a definitional statement supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: LCLs are used as a model for EBV-associated diffuse large B cell lymphoma.
source: LCLs are used extensively in research as a model for EBV-associated malignancies including diffuse large B cell lymphoma (Nichele et al., 2012; Tazzari et al., 1999) and post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder (Markasz et al., 2009; Rea et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: LCLs are used as a model for post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder.
source: LCLs are used extensively in research as a model for EBV-associated malignancies including diffuse large B cell lymphoma (Nichele et al., 2012; Tazzari et al., 1999) and post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder (Markasz et al., 2009; Rea et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: EBV is a non-mutagenic transformant in the context of LCL generation.
source: Because EBV is a non-mutagenic transformant in this context, LCLs constitute an important renewable source of human cells and genomic DNA that are used in immunological, genetic, and virology research (Çalışkan et al., 2014; Choy et al., 2008; Oh et al., 2013; Stark et al., 2010; Volkova et al., 2019).

claim: LCLs constitute an important renewable source of human cells and genomic DNA used in immunological, genetic, and virology research.
source: Because EBV is a non-mutagenic transformant in this context, LCLs constitute an important renewable source of human cells and genomic DNA that are used in immunological, genetic, and virology research (Çalışkan et al., 2014; Choy et al., 2008; Oh et al., 2013; Stark et al., 2010; Volkova et al., 2019).

claim: EBV is a double-stranded oncogenic gammaherpesvirus infecting over 90% of humans.
source: EBV is a double-stranded oncogenic gammaherpesvirus infecting over 90% of humans (Rickinson and Kieff, 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge about EBV supported by a citation.

claim: EBV typically establishes an asymptomatic persistent latent infection in episomal form within resting memory B cells in vivo.
source: In vivo, the virus typically establishes an asymptomatic persistent latent infection in episomal form (Lindahl et al., 1976; Nonoyama and Pagano, 1972) within resting memory B cells (Longnecker et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement describes established knowledge about EBV infection supported by citations.

claim: Latent EBV infection can take one of several forms, each characterized by distinct programs of viral gene expression initiated from different promoters.
source: Latent infection can take one of several forms, each characterized by distinct programs of viral gene expression initiated from different promoters (Price and Luftig, 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge about EBV latency programs supported by a citation.

claim: Classical EBV infection within resting memory B cells in vivo is characterized by the Latency I program in which expression from the Q promoter yields EBNA1.
source: For example, classical EBV infection within resting memory B cells in vivo is characterized by the Latency I program in which expression from the Q promoter yields a single viral protein, EBV Nuclear Antigen 1 (EBNA1), which functions to maintain the viral episome (Hung et al., 2001).
evidence: This describes a specific latency program supported by a citation.

claim: EBNA1 functions to maintain the viral episome.
source: For example, classical EBV infection within resting memory B cells in vivo is characterized by the Latency I program in which expression from the Q promoter yields a single viral protein, EBV Nuclear Antigen 1 (EBNA1), which functions to maintain the viral episome (Hung et al., 2001).
evidence: This describes the function of EBNA1 supported by a citation.

claim: Latency I is established after a complex progression of infection through pre-latency, Latency IIb, Latency III, and restricted forms of latency.
source: Latency I, termed 'true latency', is established only after a complex progression of infection through pre-latency, Latency IIb, Latency III, and restricted forms of latency (e.g., Latency IIa), each occurring in distinct tissues within the body (Price and Luftig, 2015).
evidence: This describes the progression of EBV latency states supported by a citation.

claim: EBV can undergo lytic reactivation as a replication strategy, which is relatively infrequent in cell culture despite being essential for transmission in vivo.
source: EBV can undergo lytic reactivation as a replication strategy, which is relatively infrequent in cell culture despite being essential for transmission in vivo (Bhende et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement about lytic reactivation is supported by a citation.

claim: In the immediate-early stage of EBV infection (the pre-latent phase), expression from the W promoter yields EBNA-LP, EBNA2, and several noncoding RNAs.
source: In the immediate-early stage of infection (the pre-latent phase), expression from the W promoter yields EBNA-LP, EBNA2, and several noncoding RNAs (EBERs, BHRF1 miRNAs, and BART miRNAs).
evidence: This describes viral gene expression during pre-latency, representing established knowledge.

claim: A brief burst of lytic gene transcription (without lytic replication) is observed during pre-latency.
source: A brief burst of lytic gene transcription (without lytic replication) is also observed during pre-latency (Woisetschlaeger et al., 1989).
evidence: This observation is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: EBNA-LP and EBNA2 protein levels increase gradually within early-infected cells, eventually leading to Latency IIb.
source: EBNA-LP and EBNA2 protein levels increase gradually within these early-infected cells, eventually leading to Latency IIb in which EBNA2 activation of the C promoter upregulates expression of EBNA1, EBNA3A, EBNA3B, EBNA3C, and additional EBNA-LP and EBNA2 proteins as well as noncoding RNAs (Alfieri et al., 1991).
evidence: This describes the progression to Latency IIb supported by a citation.

claim: Latency IIb gene products induce hyperproliferation, a period of several days during which infected B cells divide every 10–12 hr.
source: Latency IIb gene products induce hyperproliferation, a period of several days during which infected B cells divide every 10–12 hr (Nikitin et al., 2010).
evidence: This describes the hyperproliferation phase supported by a citation.

claim: During hyperproliferation, EBNA1 mediates viral genome replication while EBNA3 proteins inhibit host cell antiviral and tumor-suppression responses.
source: During hyperproliferation, EBNA1 mediates viral genome replication while EBNA3 proteins inhibit host cell antiviral and tumor-suppression responses.
evidence: This describes the functions of viral proteins during hyperproliferation, representing established knowledge.

claim: Variance in virally mediated rates of proliferation ensures that some infected cells undergo DNA damage-induced growth arrest while others continue to proliferate.
source: Variance in virally mediated rates of proliferation ensures that some infected cells undergo DNA damage-induced growth arrest (Nikitin et al., 2010; Nikitin et al., 2014) while others continue to proliferate, eventually outgrowing as immortalized LCLs.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: LCLs largely exhibit the Latency III transcriptional profile, characterized by expression of all six EBNAs and latent membrane proteins 1 and 2.
source: LCLs largely exhibit the Latency III transcriptional profile, characterized by expression of all six EBNAs (EBNA-LP, EBNA1, EBNA2, and EBNAs 3A–3C) in addition to latent membrane proteins 1 and 2 (LMP-1, LMP-2A/B) and noncoding RNAs (Young and Rickinson, 2004).

claim: In Latency III, EBNA2 stimulates expression of LMP-1, a constitutively active tumor necrosis factor receptor (TNFR) homolog.
source: In Latency III, EBNA2 stimulates expression of LMP-1, a constitutively active tumor necrosis factor receptor (TNFR) homolog (Mosialos et al., 1995).
evidence: This describes the relationship between EBNA2 and LMP-1 supported by a citation.

claim: LMP-1 signaling drives proliferation and survival via NFκB pathway activation.
source: LMP-1 signaling drives proliferation and survival via NFκB pathway activation (Devergne et al., 1996), which has been shown to be essential for LCL outgrowth (Cahir-McFarland et al., 2000).
evidence: This describes the mechanism of LMP-1 action supported by citations.

claim: NFκB pathway activation has been shown to be essential for LCL outgrowth.
source: LMP-1 signaling drives proliferation and survival via NFκB pathway activation (Devergne et al., 1996), which has been shown to be essential for LCL outgrowth (Cahir-McFarland et al., 2000).
